title: The scribe of the Granth
hook: a man writes out the Guru's hymns word for word, and keeps his own poems beside the book

segments.voice: Yesterday, amritvela, the hours before dawn, and your line was the day, in his words. That closed year two. Year three starts now.

One man reads a hymn aloud, slowly. Another dips his pen, writes down every word, and waits for the next line. Sikh tradition remembers a scene like that: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, gathering the hymns of the Gurus before him, and a learned Sikh named Bhai Gurdas writing them out into one great volume, the Adi Granth. Year three is the long story, Sikh history told slowly, and every long story needs someone who writes things down. Today: Bhai Gurdas.
screen: `ONE MAN READS.` → `ANOTHER WRITES EVERY WORD.` → `THE LONG STORY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Tradition remembers Bhai Gurdas as a relative of the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, and says he grew up close to the Gurus' household, with the hymns around him. When Guru Arjan gathered the Guru's word into one book, tradition says Bhai Gurdas held the pen while the Guru dictated. It's a strange, humble job. Your hand moves, but the words aren't yours. A scribe who adds a flourish of his own, or fixes a line he'd have written differently, has failed at the one thing a scribe is for. The whole skill is faithfulness. Now the twist. This same man was a poet with a voice of his own. He composed vars, Punjabi ballads, about the Gurus and the Sikh way of life. And he did not slip them into the volume he was writing out. His vars stand beside the Granth, never inside it. He knew which words were the Guru's and which were his, and he never blurred the line. Sikhs still sing his work. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the community's code of conduct, names the writings of Bhai Gurdas among those that may be sung as kirtan in the gurdwara, alongside gurbani, the Guru's own word. So the scribe's voice still sounds in the room, next to the book he copied, and never mistaken for it. He's also a teller of the Sikh story. His first var tells of Guru Nanak's life and travels, and over the coming days, we'll walk through it.
screen: `A RELATIVE OF GURU AMAR DAS.` · `THE SCRIBE: FAITHFUL HANDS.` · `THE POET: HIS VARS BESIDE THE GRANTH.` · `A TELLER OF THE STORY.` · then, large: `THE SCRIBE.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper, and write one line you know: the line you kept from last year, a line of the Mool Mantar, or just one word, Waheguru, slowly, letter by letter, adding nothing and decorating nothing. Then read it back once and check every word against the original, because that's the scribe's whole craft: care, and nothing of your own slipped in. If you pray, you can say the line under your breath as you write.
Bhai Gurdas, who, tradition says, wrote out the Adi Granth for Guru Arjan, and whose own vars Sikhs still sing beside it.
Your line: the scribe. Faithful hands, and his own voice kept beside the book. Day six hundred ninety-seven, and year three begins.

chat.says: Who was Bhai Gurdas? Did he write part of the Sikh scripture?
options: Tradition says he wrote out the Adi Granth for Guru Arjan; his own vars stand beside it, not inside.
Yes, he wrote his own vars into the Adi Granth as he copied it, between the Gurus' hymns.
He was the fifth Guru, so the hymns he dictated for the Adi Granth are his own.
chat.meaning: Tradition remembers him as Guru Arjan's scribe. He kept his own vars beside the Granth, never inside it, and Sikhs may sing them in kirtan.
